entry.evidence: However, it is unclear whether these deep-carbon reservoirs can be locally remobilized on shorter-term timescales.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), with the PDF for figure content

steps.action: The authors recall their earlier surface-wave tomography and petrological work, which imaged a shear-wave low-velocity anomaly beneath the Po Plain. They read that anomaly as a carbon reservoir in the asthenospheric mantle wedge.
steps.quote: provides evidence of active carbon sequestration in the asthenospheric mantle above the European slab

steps.action: They pose the question of whether this deep carbon can be mobilized on timescales much shorter than plate-tectonic cycles.
steps.quote: we explore the possibility that deep carbon could be variably mobilized on much shorter timescales relevant to anthropogenic processes

steps.action: They choose the volumetric component of earthquake moment tensors as the observable for melt and fluid migration, taking this link from published work.
steps.quote: [...] migration within the Earth can be revealed by the volumetric components of earthquake moment tensors

steps.action: They take the 17 December 2020 earthquake beneath almost aseismic Milan, a live one-off event, as the found conditions for the test.
steps.quote: The seismic event that occurred beneath Milan on the 17th of December 2020 at 15:59:22 UTC (Fig. 1a) provides an invaluable opportunity

steps.action: They locate the hypocentre at 66 ± 20 km depth in the Adriatic lithospheric mantle, with moment magnitude 4.6 ± 0.3; E.B. and G.F.P. did the location.
steps.quote: The hypocenter of the analyzed 4.6 ± 0.3 moment magnitude earthquake is located in the lithospheric mantle of the Adriatic plate

steps.action: They read their earlier tomography model at the source location. Shear-wave velocities there are slightly lower than in typical Adriatic lithospheric mantle (4.25–4.55 vs 4.50–4.80 km/s).
steps.quote: [...] event originated in a region with shear-wave velocities that are slightly lower than those generally observed in the lithospheric mantle

steps.action: They propose that minor melt is present at the source. They interpret an explosive moment-tensor component as rapid CO2 release when carbon-rich melts rising along upper-mantle shear zones exit the carbonate stability field.
steps.quote: This is interpreted as the effect of rapid CO2 release when carbon-rich melts migrating along upper-mantle shear zones exit the carbonate stability field.

steps.action: They invert the full source moment tensor with the INPAR point-source method. INPAR uses modal-summation Green's functions, MTRF deconvolution, factorization and a genetic algorithm (Methods §3.1 ¶1) and is fed the dominant part of regional waveforms. The inversion returns a strike-slip double couple plus an explosive component (35% V, 64% DC, 1% CLVD), with the volumetric part lasting longer.
steps.quote: The INPAR inversion of the Milan earthquake returned a double-couple component associated with a major explosive component

steps.action: They assess the solution with two checks. The confidence area of the total-mechanism vector comes from the genetic-algorithm population. They also check consistency with first-motion polarities, which a pure double-couple mechanism would not fit.
steps.quote: The small confidence area of vector L denotes the robustness of the solution and the reliability of the volumetric component.

steps.action: They compare the deviatoric strike-slip mechanism with earlier anomalously deep Adriatic-mantle earthquakes beneath the western Po Plain, which their own group described.
steps.quote: which are common to most anomalously deep earthquakes sourced in the Adriatic mantle and previously described in the western Po Plain

steps.action: They estimate the source volume change from the isotropic moment and Lamé parameters under three source models: fluid, crack-like and compact (Methods §3.2 ¶1). The result is ΔV ≈ 1.3–2.2 × 10^4 m3, with the compact case as the lower bound.
steps.quote: The latter value provides a lower bound for volume-change estimates based on earthquake source moment-tensor analysis

steps.action: They build a pressure–temperature path (Fig. 3) from cited experimental solidi and a mantle geotherm. It implies that thermal perturbations of a few tens of degrees can trigger incipient melting of carbonated peridotite shallower than ~180 km.
steps.quote: This implies that minor thermal perturbations—on the order of a few tens of degrees—may induce carbonated peridotite incipient melting

steps.action: They exclude a large thermal perturbation such as a mantle plume. A plume would remobilize melt over hundreds of kilometres in map view, which the tomography does not show.
steps.quote: Large thermal perturbations, such as those associated with a mantle plume, would determine melt remobilization over hundreds of kilometers in map view, unlike observed

steps.action: They compare the double-couple component with published N-S hypocentre alignments and strike-slip focal solutions that indicate sinistral lithospheric faults.
steps.quote: in agreement with the double-couple component returned by the Milan earthquake

steps.action: They add an auxiliary hypothesis: ductile strike-slip shear zones, undetectable seismically, carry the lithospheric faults down into the uppermost asthenosphere.
steps.quote: These shear zones likely extend to the uppermost part of the asthenospheric mantle

steps.action: They check the shear-zone auxiliary against independent SKS splitting data from their earlier synthesis. The NNE-SSW fast axes match the nodal-plane orientations.
steps.quote: which are consistent with the orientation of nodal planes retrieved for the Milan earthquake

steps.action: They derive from cited viscous-heating and conduction arguments that km-thick shear zones heat up progressively. They postulate that this heating is enough to remobilize carbon-rich melts, which then rise until decarbonation releases CO2.
steps.quote: we postulate that this localized temperature increase is sufficient to locally remobilize carbon-rich melts in the uppermost part of the asthenosphere

steps.action: They compare the predicted carbonate-stability loop in the solidus at ~2 GPa with the observed hypocentral depth.
steps.quote: consistent with the hypocentral depth of the explosive earthquake analyzed in this work

steps.action: They retain a causal link between the inferred CO2 release and the volume increase from the moment tensor.
steps.quote: We suggest a causal relationship between the inferred CO2 release and the volume increase revealed by earthquake source moment-tensor analysis.

steps.action: They convert the compact-source volume to a CO2 mass (Methods §3.3 ¶1). The conversion uses an equivalent sphere of radius 15 m and an assumed CO2 density of 1100 kg/m3 at 2–2.5 GPa and 800–900 °C. The result is a lower bound of ~17,000 t.
steps.quote: The lower-bound amount of degassed CO2 inferred for the Milan earthquake is ~17,000 tons

steps.action: They compare the estimated CO2 output with published daily emissions of the most actively degassing volcanoes (Nyiragongo–Nyamuragira, Etna).
steps.quote: [...] CO2 emitted daily by the most actively degassing volcanoes in the world

steps.action: They conclude that cold-subduction asthenospheric carbon reservoirs can be remobilized nearly instantaneously by tectonics, contributing episodically to atmospheric CO2. They do so while noting that direct CO2 measurements are not available.
steps.quote: our findings demonstrate that asthenospheric-mantle carbon reservoirs formed during cold subduction can experience nearly “instantaneous” remobilization driven by tectonics

tree.answer: An anomalously deep (66 km) mantle earthquake beneath almost aseismic Milan, above an imaged carbon reservoir
No; the explosive component is inferred by moment-tensor inversion and CO2 release is not measured
Whether deep carbon can be remobilized on short timescales and outgassed
Only for the heat source: localized shear-zone heating vs a mantle plume; no rival origins for the volumetric component are stated
A plume predicts melt remobilization over hundreds of km in map view; the carbonate loop at ~2 GPa predicts the source depth

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Not used; earlier deep Adriatic earthquakes are cited for mechanism only, and their volumetric components are not analysed
Partly: GA confidence area, polarity consistency, three volume-change models, SKS consistency; no synthetic or structural-model tests
Kept as the best explanation: CO2 release from remobilized carbon-rich melts

end.claim: The major explosive component of the Milan earthquake moment tensor reflects rapid release of at least ~17,000 t of CO2 as carbon-rich melts, remobilized along upper-mantle shear zones, exit the carbonate stability field.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the INPAR full moment-tensor inversion returning a one-third explosive volumetric component, there would be no volume change, no CO2 estimate and no outgassing claim.

gates.evidence: Action: the inversion was run 'In order to detect a potential volumetric component' (§2.1 ¶1), motivated by the carbon-release question. The waveforms, however, were archived network data, not acquired for the purpose. Claim: the inversion could have returned no volumetric component, and the hypocentral depth could have mismatched the ~2 GPa loop. The CO2 interpretation itself was not tested against rival origins of the isotropic component, and the CO2 release was not measured (§2.3 ¶3). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Genetic algorithm used to obtain the preferred solution and confidence areas of source parameters
Density of CO2 fluid (1100 kg/m3) at 2–2.5 GPa and 800–900 °C used to convert volume to mass

limits:
1. No peer-review file was supplied, although the paper states that reviewer reports exist, so no review sequence is coded and tree question 9 is not answered.

2. The supplementary material (stations, Supplementary Fig. 1, Tables 1–3) was not supplied.

3. The main text reports no synthetic test of whether structural mismodelling, sparse station coverage or noise could produce a spurious isotropic component. It also reports no inversion with alternative velocity models or station subsets. Rivals for the volumetric component are not stated or tested; the paper itself cites artefact concerns (ref. 26), phase transformations and other fluid processes.

4. The only excluded rival is a mantle plume as the heat source.

5. The CO2 release is inferred, not measured (§2.3 ¶3). The ~17,000 t figure has no stated uncertainty and depends on an assumed density and the compact-source model.

6. The text is internally inconsistent on bounds: §2.1 ¶3 calls the crack-like case 'higher', while §3.2 ¶1 names the fluid case as the upper bound.

7. Sub-claims and their statuses:
- Explosive component of 35% of the tensor: estimate_with_resolution (GA confidence area).
- ΔV ≈ 1.3–2.2 × 10^4 m3: estimate_with_resolution (range across source assumptions).
- CO2 ≥ ~17,000 t: estimate given as a lower bound only.
- Shear-heating remobilization mechanism: best_explanation, postulated (§2.3 ¶1).
- Episodic atmospheric contribution: inference from a single event.

8. Composition is none_fits. The walk rests on one found event plus consistency with cited, largely the authors' own, data sets (tomography, hypocentre alignments, SKS splitting, experimental solidi). There are no repeated independent traces, no crucial test among rivals and no regularity fit.

9. Coding inferences:
- The SKS comparison is coded as a replication check performed here, because the comparison is the paper's; the data are cited. It is a consistency argument for an auxiliary, not for the main claim.
- Treating the GA confidence area as a robustness check is the coder's inference.

disagreements.target: Position that subduction-sequestered deep carbon is released on plate-tectonic timescales during continental breakup (refs 3, 5, 15–19)
disagreements.support: A single mantle earthquake with an explosive component is interpreted as short-timescale, tectonically driven remobilization and outgassing of the same reservoir.
disagreements.quote: Notwithstanding the impact of these processes on timescales typical of plate-tectonic cycles

disagreements.target: General finding that isotropic components are negligible in most tectonic earthquakes, being seen mainly in volcanic zones (refs 20, 25, [...]
disagreements.support: The INPAR inversion of a non-volcanic mantle earthquake returns a 35% explosive volumetric component with a small confidence area.
disagreements.quote: Although isotropic components are generally negligible in most tectonic earthquakes

disagreements.target: View that diffuse fault-controlled carbon outgassing matters in continental rifts and transform faults (refs 44, 45)
disagreements.support: The inferred ~17,000 t CO2 release beneath Milan is used to extend diffuse fault and shear-zone outgassing to active continental margins.
disagreements.quote: diffuse carbon outgassing through faults and shear zones is a relevant process, not only in continental rifts and transform faults

alternatives_considered.chosen: Compact source, used as the lower bound (ΔV ≈ 1.3 × 10^4 m3) and for the CO2 conversion
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Volumetric change in a fluid; crack-like rupture with partly tensile components (ΔV ≈ 2.2 × 10^4 m3)
alternatives_considered.reason: Expected for concentrated phase transformations; gives a lower bound

alternatives_considered.chosen: Localized thermal perturbations from upper-mantle shear-zone activity
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Large thermal perturbations such as those of a mantle plume
alternatives_considered.reason: A plume would remobilize melt over hundreds of kilometres in map view, unlike the tomography

alternatives_considered.chosen: CO2 fluid in equilibrium with lithostatic pressure (density 1100 kg/m3)
